narrative:
The model predicts you have a 24% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you succeed.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your plans for higher education, your history of past failures, and your reason for choosing this school. Wanting to pursue higher education actually worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward passing. However, this positive influence was outweighed by two other important elements that pulled the outcome toward failing.

Having already failed one class in the past was the second strongest factor and increased the risk of failing this year, especially since students who passed had zero previous failures on average. Your reason for choosing this school—being close to home—was the third most influential factor and also nudged the prediction toward failing, unlike most students who passed and typically chose the school for its course offerings or reputation.

To improve, you should focus on preventing any further setbacks by attending every class, catching up on missed material quickly, and building consistent daily study habits. Even though you want to continue your education after this year, turning around your attendance and study routine now will be the most practical way to avoid repeating a failure and remove the need for remedial courses. (248 words)
